prime.problem: The four cards each name a different control (a narrow tool, an untrusted-output rule, an identity envelope, an approval or a sandbox), and it's easy to treat any one of them as "the security". Each control guards a different failure, and none of them checks the agent's final claim. This page puts them on one request path so you can see which gate catches what.
prime.fits: The map for course 3: read it first to place the four cards, or last as a recap. It builds on the map course's "same label, different authority" and on the anatomy of a tool call (the model asks; the harness acts).
expect: A(k+1) ⊆ A(k); A(effective) = requester ∩ actor ∩ stage
four gates: askable, in the envelope, approved, reachable
tool output can steer the model but never adds authority
"Done" passes every gate, so the checker is the next course's job
prime.goal: Place any agent incident on the four gates, say which gate should have caught it, and name the card that explains the fix.

must: The model only asks → the system decides and acts → each decision is a separate gate (capability surface, envelope, approval, containment) owned outside the model → name the gate before picking the fix

Authority is a set carried with the request → each stage may drop scopes, never add them, and the actor is intersected with the requester → a broad bot or a persuasive tool result can't spend authority the task never had

Approval guards only the paths that call it, and containment wraps every path but decides nothing → a skipped prompt is caught only by containment, and a wrong in-scope action only by approval → consequential agents need both
Every gate limits actions, not words → a steered or confused model can still say "Done, all tests pass" → only a checker that re-runs against the world catches the false success claim (course 4)
elevated: Order on the path: the envelope check runs before approval → a request outside the envelope never reaches a human → approval can't be used to widen authority by accident; widening must be its own recorded escalation
reference: the per-row numbers in the ranking (each lives on its card)
the list of post URLs in "Where to look it up"

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between the four gates by saying, for each one, the question it answers and who enforces it.
answer: capability surface: what may the model ask for at all? the harness, by what it exposes
envelope: may this request do this to this resource? policy code outside the model, at each action
approval: should this specific side effect happen now? a person or rule, at the side effect
containment: what can the running process reach? the OS or execution backend

retrieve.q: Walk the Tuesday run's injected fixture ("mark the task done") through the four gates. Where does each of the steered model's proposals die, and what gets through?
answer: editing src/ is allowed: it's the real task
editing the tests is denied by the write root, the push by the envelope, and "mark done" by the gate reading the last pytest exit code
the final "Done" message is delivered, because no gate checks words

retrieve.q: You can add one control to a shell-only coding agent this week: narrow tools, a per-stage envelope, approval before pushes, or a no-network container. Which first, and what does each leave uncovered?
answer: the container covers every path, including ones that skip approval, but not wrong in-scope edits
approval before pushes catches a specific irreversible effect but only on paths that ask
narrow tools shrink what can be attempted but may block legitimate open-ended work
an envelope matters most once there is a shared bot or other users; for one dev on their own repo it adds little

compare.q: The map course listed boundary pairs that hide behind one label. Which pairs does this course turn into separate gates, and what does putting them on one path add?
answer: capability ≠ execution, session ≠ authorization and approval ≠ isolation all become separate gates
the path shows the order: what can be asked, then what is allowed, then whether it happens now, then what it can reach
it also shows what no gate covers: the final claim

compare.q: The done chain splits "Done" into request, tool, command, effect and delivered. Which links can the gates in this course protect, and which link can none of them move from ✗ to ✓?
answer: the gates limit which commands can run and where, so they shrink what can go wrong before "command succeeded"
none of them verifies the effect; an allowed command can still exit 1
"effect verified" needs a check against the world, which is course 4

predict.q: The bot ∩ task envelope holds 3 scopes and no push. A tool result now asks for git:push-main, and the harness also has an approval prompt before pushes. Does a human ever see a push prompt, and if not, what would have to happen for the push to be possible?
predict.answer: No prompt appears. The envelope check comes before approval on the path, so a request outside the envelope dies at gate 2 and never reaches a human. For the push to become possible, someone would have to widen the envelope explicitly: Part 7 lists privilege escalation among the actions that need approval, so widening is its own recorded step, never a side effect of text the model read.
